analogy.p: A pure substance is a jar containing only sugar: every grain is the same. A mixture is a bag of mixed sweets thrown together in any amounts: you can still see and pick out each type. A formulation is a cake recipe: the same ingredients, but each is weighed carefully and chosen for a job (flour for structure, sugar for sweetness, egg to bind), so every cake turns out the same. The analogy breaks down because in baking the ingredients react chemically and cannot be separated again, whereas the components of a chemical formulation are generally mixed but not chemically joined.
analogy.t: Pure substance, mixture and formulation as kitchen ingredients

bullets: **Pure substance** = a single element or compound not mixed with any other substance.
Examples of pure elements: oxygen, copper, sulfur. Examples of pure compounds: water, sodium chloride, carbon dioxide.
In a pure substance every particle is the same type: the same atoms (element) or the same molecules/ions in a fixed ratio (compound).
Everyday "pure" (e.g. pure milk, pure orange juice, pure air) describes something natural or unadulterated, but it is almost always a **mixture** chemically.
A pure substance cannot be separated into other substances by physical methods such as filtering, distillation or chromatography.
Compounds can only be broken down into elements by **chemical reactions**, whereas mixtures can be separated by **physical** methods.
Purity matters in industry: medicines, food additives and electronics need substances of known purity so they are safe and work reliably.
core.p: In everyday language **pure** means "natural" or "nothing added" (pure orange juice, pure spring water). In chemistry it has a much stricter meaning. A **pure substance** is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. Pure orange juice is therefore not chemically pure, because it contains water, sugars, acids, vitamins and many other compounds. Examiners reward you for stating the chemical meaning and for contrasting it with the everyday meaning.

bullets: **Element**: one type of atom only (e.g. Fe, O2). Cannot be broken down chemically.
**Compound**: different atoms chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (e.g. H2O is always 2 H : 1 O). Properties differ from the elements it contains.
**Mixture**: no chemical bonds between the different substances; amounts can vary (air, sea water, crude oil, alloys).
Components of a mixture keep their **own chemical properties**, e.g. iron filings mixed with sulfur are still attracted to a magnet; iron sulfide (a compound) is not.
Making a mixture involves no chemical reaction and usually no energy change; making a compound is a chemical reaction.
Elements and compounds are pure substances; a mixture is NOT a pure substance.
Particle diagrams: pure element = all circles identical; compound = identical groups of joined different circles; mixture = different particles (or groups) scattered with no fixed ratio.
core.p: To decide whether something is a pure substance you must be able to tell elements, compounds and mixtures apart. An element contains only one type of atom. A compound contains two or more different elements chemically joined in a fixed proportion by bonds. A mixture contains two or more substances (elements and/or compounds) that are **not chemically joined**, so each keeps its own properties and they can be present in any proportion.

bullets: Pure ice melts at exactly **0 °C**; pure water freezes at 0 °C (at normal atmospheric pressure).
Pure substances have a **sharp** melting point: the whole sample melts over a very narrow range (about 1 °C or less).
Each pure substance has its own **fixed** melting point, so the value can identify an unknown solid when compared with a data table.
On a temperature-time graph, melting is shown by a flat horizontal line (plateau) because energy is used to break intermolecular forces/bonds, not to raise temperature.
Pure substances have **fixed** melting points; this also means that a sample whose melting point matches the data-book value is probably pure and is probably that substance.
A sample is heated slowly near the melting point so the thermometer and sample stay at the same temperature, giving an accurate reading.
core.p: A pure substance melts at one specific temperature. During melting the energy supplied is used to overcome the forces holding the particles in the solid structure, so the temperature stays constant until all the solid has melted. This is why a heating curve for a pure substance shows a flat plateau. The melting point is a characteristic property, which means it can be used like a fingerprint to identify the substance by comparing with data-book values.

bullets: Pure water boils at **100 °C** at normal atmospheric pressure.
A pure liquid has a single, fixed boiling point; this is used for identification by comparing with data-book values.

A mixture of liquids has no single boiling point: the component with the lowest boiling point boils off first, and the temperature rises as the mixture boils. This is how **fractional distillation** works.
Dissolving a substance in water normally makes it boil at a temperature above 100 °C and over a range, so impure water does not boil sharply at 100 °C.
The boiling point depends on pressure, so data-book values are quoted at standard atmospheric pressure.
Flat plateaus on a heating curve are at the melting point and boiling point only for pure substances.
core.p: In the same way, a pure liquid boils at one fixed temperature (at a given pressure). While it boils, energy is used to separate the particles completely into a gas so the temperature stays constant. Pure water boils at **100 °C** at normal atmospheric pressure. A mixture of liquids, or a liquid with something dissolved in it, boils over a range of temperatures or at a different temperature, which is why boiling data are also used to test purity.

bullets: Impure substance: melts **over a range** of temperatures rather than at a single temperature.
The melting point of an impure sample is usually **lower** than that of the pure substance (impurities disrupt the regular arrangement of particles in the solid).
The more impurity present, the lower the melting point and the wider the range.
Boiling points of impure liquids are usually changed too and boiling happens over a range, not at one fixed temperature.
To judge purity, **compare** the measured value with the data-book value for the pure substance: matching and sharp suggests pure.
Always quote numbers when interpreting: e.g. "it melts between 74 and 79 °C, a range of 5 °C, and below the data value of 80 °C, so it is impure".
core.h: How impurities change melting and boiling points
core.p: Using melting and boiling data to check purity is a key skill. An impure sample (a mixture) behaves differently from the pure substance in two ways: the melting temperature is usually **lower** than the data-book value, and the sample melts gradually over a **range** of temperatures instead of at a single sharp temperature. Because the sample has a range rather than a fixed value, you can see immediately on a graph that it is a mixture.

bullets: Step 1: find the melting range (highest minus lowest temperature) and decide if it is sharp (about 1 °C) or wide.
Step 2: compare with the data-book melting point of the pure substance.
Step 3: conclude: sharp and matching = pure; wide range and/or lower = impure (mixture).
To identify an unknown, look for the data-book substance whose melting point matches the sharp value.
If two unknowns have the same melting point, a single test may not tell them apart; a second property (e.g. boiling point, or a chemical test) is needed.
On a heating curve, count the plateaus: a pure substance heated from solid to gas shows two plateaus (melting and boiling).
A heating curve for a mixture shows no clear flat plateau; the temperature keeps rising slowly during melting.
core.p: Exam questions often give a table of melting points or a graph and ask whether a substance is pure or which substance it is. Work through three checks: is the melting range narrow, does the value match the data book, and is any value lower than the data-book value. Writing all three in your answer secures the marks. If a question asks which of two samples is purer, the one that melts over the narrower range and closer to the true melting point is the purer.

bullets: **Formulation** = a mixture designed as a useful product, made by mixing components in carefully measured quantities.
Each ingredient is chosen to give the product a **particular property** needed for its use.
The quantities are controlled so that every batch has the same properties (consistent quality).
Formulations are made by mixing, not by chemical reactions between the components.
Many useful products are formulations, so the composition on the label gives the proportions of components.
Compare: ordinary mixtures such as sea water or air are not designed or made in measured quantities for a purpose.
core.p: A **formulation** is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product. It is made by following a recipe so that the components are present in **carefully measured quantities**, which gives the product the right properties for its job. Each component has a specific role. Formulations are therefore not random mixtures: the chemist chooses what to add and how much, to make something that works well, is safe and is cost effective.

bullets: **Fuels**: e.g. petrol is a blend of hydrocarbons chosen so it ignites well and flows properly in engines in different weather.
**Cleaning agents**: contain detergent (removes grease), water or a solvent and often other additives such as fragrance.
**Paints**: pigment (colour), binder (holds pigment and forms a film), solvent (makes it spreadable, then evaporates), additives (e.g. to stop mould).
**Medicines**: the active ingredient (drug) plus other substances that help it be taken, e.g. to bind the tablet or to control release; the dose is carefully controlled.
**Alloys**: mixtures of metals (or a metal and a non-metal) with properties designed for a use, e.g. brass is copper with zinc; steel is iron with carbon.
**Fertilisers**: contain compounds supplying nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in carefully measured proportions for crops.
**Foods**: recipes such as bread or a cake use measured quantities of ingredients; food additives preserve or flavour it.
core.p: The specification lists fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods as formulations. You should be able to give an example and explain, in general terms, what the different components do. The key principle in each is the same: different components each contribute a useful property, and the amounts are controlled to make the product work.

bullets: Too much active ingredient in a medicine could be harmful; too little would not treat the illness.
Too little binder in paint means the pigment does not stick; too much solvent makes it too runny.
An alloy with the wrong proportion of carbon in steel would have the wrong hardness and strength.
A fertiliser with the wrong ratio of N, P and K may not give the plant what it needs.
Controlled amounts give **consistent** products, batch after batch, which customers and regulators rely on.
Formulations are developed by experimenting with different proportions and testing the properties.
core.h: Why quantities must be carefully controlled
core.p: The reason a formulation works is that its composition is controlled. If the quantity of one component is too high or too low, the properties of the product change, and it might not do its job or might even be unsafe. This is why manufacturers use precise measuring and quality control, and why the quantities of each component are written down in the recipe.

bullets: Pure substance: one substance only; fixed sharp melting and boiling point (e.g. distilled water, pure copper).
Mixture: more than one substance, not bonded, any proportions, melts/boils over a range (e.g. sea water, air, crude oil).
Formulation: a mixture designed for a use, in measured quantities (e.g. paint, medicine, fertiliser, alloy such as brass).
Alloys are **mixtures**, not compounds, because the metals are not chemically bonded in fixed ratios; they are also formulations because they are designed.
Key justification words: "not chemically bonded", "fixed ratio", "carefully measured quantities", "designed for a particular use".
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods (filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation, chromatography); see the separation techniques topic.
core.h: Distinguishing pure substances, mixtures and formulations
core.p: A common exam trap is to confuse the three terms. All formulations are mixtures, but not all mixtures are formulations. A pure substance is a single element or compound. A mixture is any combination of substances that are not chemically joined. A formulation is a mixture with a purpose and carefully measured quantities. Being able to place a named example in the correct category and justify it is a typical 2 to 3 mark question.

bullets: One spot on the chromatogram = a pure substance (in that solvent).
Two or more spots = a mixture (so not a pure substance).
Formulations such as food colourings and inks can be analysed by chromatography to show which dyes they contain.
To be confident a substance is pure, test it in more than one solvent: still one spot each time.
Chromatography is quick and needs only a tiny sample, but does not give melting point data.
Different methods can be used together for stronger evidence about purity.
core.p: Besides melting and boiling points, **chromatography** is another way to test purity. A pure substance produces a single spot in every solvent, whereas a mixture produces more than one spot. This links to the next topic (chromatography and Rf values), where you will measure distances and calculate Rf. Remember that chromatography can separate and identify the components of formulations such as inks, dyes and food colourings.

bullets: Compound formulae show **fixed ratios**; a mixture has no formula.
Changes of state are physical changes; the particle model explains why pure substances have fixed melting and boiling points.
Purification: crystallisation and distillation produce purer samples; melting point checks their purity afterwards.
Alloys link to metals and their uses: the different-sized atoms disturb layers so alloys are harder than pure metals.
Fuels link to crude oil and fractional distillation: fractions are mixtures of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points.
Water treatment: potable water is not pure water; it is safe to drink but contains dissolved substances.
Particle explanation: in an impure solid the regular lattice is disrupted, so less energy is needed to start melting.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher-tier thinking
core.p: This topic links to several other parts of the specification. The same ideas of fixed and variable composition appear in the structure and bonding topics (a compound has a fixed formula), in the separation methods used to purify products, and in industry topics such as the Haber process where purity and quantities matter. At higher grades, expect to explain the **why** with particles: melting is when thermal energy overcomes the forces between particles; impurities disrupt the regular structure and so lower the melting point.

exam: 1 mark definitions: "A pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance." Learn this word for word.
2 mark "explain how melting point shows purity": pure substance has a fixed/sharp melting point; impure melts over a range (and at a lower temperature).
Command word 'Describe' on a graph: say what the line does (flat plateau at melting point, then rises) and quote temperatures.
For data questions always compare the measured value with the data-book value and quote the numbers.
Define formulation: "a mixture designed as a useful product, made by mixing components in carefully measured quantities" (2 marks: designed for a purpose + measured quantities).
Give an example AND a use of each component to score full marks on 'explain why paint is a formulation'.
3 mark 'compare' answers need a point about each substance and a link word (whereas, but).
If asked 'why must quantities be controlled?': say the properties change if amounts change, so the product might not work or might be unsafe.
Use particle language for 4 to 6 mark answers: impurities disrupt the regular lattice so melting happens at lower temperatures over a range.
Identify mixtures in particle diagrams: different particles not joined; compounds show joined unlike atoms.
Do not write 'it is pure because it is natural'; examiners only credit the chemical meaning.
Check units: temperatures in °C and ranges as a difference of two numbers.

mistakes.r: In chemistry a pure substance is a single element or compound not mixed with any other substance.
mistakes.w: Pure means it has nothing added or is natural, e.g. pure orange juice.

mistakes.r: Pure substances melt at a fixed, sharp temperature; the value can be high or low depending on the substance.
mistakes.w: Pure substances melt at a high temperature.

mistakes.r: Impurities usually lower the melting point and make the sample melt over a range.
The substances in a mixture are not chemically joined, so no reaction is involved in making it.
mistakes.w: A mixture has a chemical reaction between the substances.

mistakes.r: A formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product, with components in carefully measured quantities.
Alloys are mixtures (formulations) of metals; the atoms are not chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
The temperature stays constant (plateau) during melting; energy overcomes forces between particles.
mistakes.w: The temperature goes up during melting of a pure substance.

mistakes.r: A sharp melting point matching the data book suggests it is pure; use more than one test for confidence.
mistakes.w: One method (melting point) proves a substance is pure.

summary: You must know that a pure substance is a single element or compound not mixed with any other substance, and use melting and boiling point data to tell pure substances from mixtures. You also need to know that a formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product with carefully measured quantities, and give examples such as fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. These ideas underpin purification, analysis and industrial chemistry.

terms.d: A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
A substance made of one type of atom only.
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically joined in a fixed proportion.
Two or more substances (elements and/or compounds) that are not chemically joined together.
A mixture that has been designed as a useful product, made from components in carefully measured quantities.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid; fixed and sharp for a pure substance.
The temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas; fixed for a pure substance at a given pressure.
The spread of temperatures over which an impure solid melts, instead of one sharp temperature.
An unwanted substance mixed with a pure substance.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, designed for useful properties.
A formulation (e.g. petrol) containing substances chosen to release energy usefully when burned.
A formulation containing compounds that supply elements such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to plants.
The accepted melting or boiling point of a pure substance, used for comparison.
A flat section of a temperature-time graph during a change of state, where heat is used to change state, not temperature.
A technique used to separate the substances in a mixture and to test purity; a pure substance gives one spot.

worked.ans: The sample is impure (a mixture). It melts over a range of 5 °C rather than at one sharp temperature, and below the pure melting point of 80 °C.
worked.q: A student heated an unknown white solid and recorded that it melted between 74 °C and 79 °C. The data book value for the pure substance is 80 °C. State, with reasons, whether the sample is pure. (3 marks)
steps: Melting range = 79 − 74 = 5 °C, which is wide (a pure substance melts at one sharp temperature).
The whole range is below the data-book value of 80 °C (impurities lower the melting point).
So the sample does not behave as a pure substance.

worked.ans: X is probably pure benzoic acid because it melts sharply at the data-book value. A second test, such as chromatography (one spot, matching Rf) or a boiling point check, would give more confidence.
worked.q: Substance X melts at exactly 122 °C (sharp). The data book gives benzoic acid at 122 °C and another solid at 135 °C. What can the student conclude and what further test would add confidence? (3 marks)
steps: Sharp melting point suggests X is pure.
Matches 122 °C, so X is probably benzoic acid, not the 135 °C solid.
Evidence is stronger with a second test, because different substances can have the same melting point.

worked.ans: Paint is a mixture designed for a use. It contains pigment for colour, a binder to make it stick and form a film, a solvent to make it spreadable and additives, mixed in carefully measured quantities so that every batch has the right properties.
worked.q: Explain why emulsion paint is called a formulation. (4 marks)
steps: Define: a formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product.
Components: pigment, binder, solvent and additives are mixed.
Roles: pigment gives colour, binder holds it on the wall, solvent spreads it.
Quantities: each is added in carefully measured amounts.
